svg.aria-label: Diagram: Amazon RDS for Oracle now lets you turn off automatic minor version upgrades on new and existing DB instances that use the JVM, Spatial, Locator or OLAP option, which previously mandated the setting. What changed is not the upgrade but who is responsible for it: AWS states that you now decide when to apply minor version upgrades, and recommends in the same announcement that you apply new minor versions regularly so your DB instances keep the latest Oracle security fixes. The documented reason to want the setting off is Multi-AZ behaviour: for an engine upgrade Amazon RDS modifies both primary and secondary DB instances at the same time, both are unavailable, and the operation causes downtime until the upgrade is complete, while the maintenance window determines when operations start but does not limit their total run time. AWS names a third option between leaving it on and turning it off, the AWS Organizations upgrade rollout policy, which controls the sequence in which environments receive updates while automatic upgrades stay enabled. The diagram closes by noting that a mandate fails loudly at a time AWS chose while a recommendation fails silently over months in a backlog, so the replacement obligation needs an owner and a drift threshold.
svg.title: A platform-enforced obligation became a customer-held one
svg.text: The upgrade did not become optional. The obligation did.
RDS for Oracle — JVM, Spatial, Locator and OLAP no longer mandate automatic minor version upgrades.
BEFORE — the platform held it
These four options mandated the setting. Upgrades
arrived in the weekly maintenance window.
Fails loudly, at a time AWS chose.
AFTER — you hold it
“With this change, you decide when to apply minor
version upgrades to DB instances using these options.”
Fails silently, over months, in a backlog.
AWS attaches the duty to the freedom, in the same announcement
“we recommend that you apply new minor versions regularly so your DB instances keep the latest Oracle security fixes”
Why anyone wants it off — and this part is documented, not folklore
“Amazon RDS modifies both primary and secondary DB instances at the same time … both are
unavailable during the upgrade. This operation causes downtime until the upgrade is complete.”
And the window starts the work without containing it: it “doesn’t limit the total run time of these operations”.
The third option, which is probably the right one
Keep automatic upgrades on and “use AWS Organizations upgrade rollout policy” to control the sequence in
which environments receive updates. Sequencing, without anyone taking custody of Oracle patching.
If you turn it off, create the replacement obligation in the same change.
An owner, a recurring check for available minor versions, and a maximum drift you will tolerate. Without a
threshold, “regularly” resolves to whenever somebody is worried.
Leave it on in non-production: free early warning, on instances where an unplanned restart costs nothing.
